1:
The survey is over and the vision changes register. Gill notes only the movement: the dimensions of the building being finished, the prophet’s divine guide brings him from the wall he last measured back to the gate he was taken to first. Clarke sets out the whole chapter in a sentence: the glory returning to the temple, God promising to fix his residence there if the people repent and forsake the sins that caused him to depart, then the measures of the altar and its ordinances. Henry marks the change of altitude. After the prophet has patiently surveyed the temple, the greatest glory of this earth, he is admitted to a higher form and honoured with a sight of the glories of the upper world, as though it were said to him, Come up hither. He has seen the house, and seen it spacious and splendid; but until the glory of God comes into it, Henry says, it is like the dead bodies of an earlier vision, which had no breath till the Spirit of life entered them. Now he sees the house filled.

Whose glory it is gets three answers that overlap without quite meeting. Henry takes it as the glory of the God of Israel, the God in covenant with Israel whom they serve and worship, and sharpens the phrase by contrast: the idols of the heathen have no glory but what they owe to the goldsmith or the painter. Gill reads the same title as covering both the covenant God of literal Israel and the Father of the whole spiritual Israel, his elect, whether Jews or Gentiles; but he holds that Christ is here meant, the brightness of his Father’s glory, who has the same attributes and names and worship as the Father, and in whom as Mediator the glory of all the divine perfections is displayed. Clarke identifies the appearance instead with what the prophet had already seen, the chariot of cherubim and wheels at the river Chebar, now coming from the east to enter the eastern gate and thence to shine out upon the whole earth.

Why it comes from the east is answered differently by each. Wesley gives the plainest reason, that when the glory departed it went eastward, and now that it returns it comes from the east. Henry says the glory came from the east and that this is why the prophet was brought to the gate that leads eastward, to expect its approach there; and he reads the quarter as a sign, since Christ’s star was seen in the east and he is the morning star and the sun of righteousness. Gill argues from the title, the coming from the east agreeing with Christ as the rising sun of righteousness, with his incarnation in the east where his star appeared, and with the Gospel having first come and been first preached there and churches first planted. Clarke widens it into a law of history and asks whether there is not a mystery in it: all knowledge, all religion, and all arts and sciences have travelled with the course of the sun, from east to west; from that quarter the divine glory at first came, and thence the rays of divine light continue to diffuse themselves over the face of the earth, and thence came the Bible, the prophets, the apostles and the first missionaries who brought the knowledge of God to Europe. On the sound Henry hears the power of the word: the voice was like a noise of many waters, heard very far and making impressions, the noise of purling streams being grateful and that of a roaring sea dreadful, and the gospel in whose glory Christ shines was to be proclaimed aloud. Wesley enters a caution against taking it for weather, since though thunder is sometimes meant by the voice of God, here it was an articulate voice.
3:
That the appearance was not new is agreed. Gill says the form in which the glory now appeared was like what the prophet had seen in the visions recorded earlier in the book, in each of which there was the likeness of a throne and on it the appearance of the glory of God. Ellicott says the same more briefly, that the manifestation of divine glory to this prophet was the same throughout. On the harder phrase about coming to destroy the city, Ellicott and Wesley agree that it means coming to announce the destruction, Wesley putting it as a declaration that their sins would ruin their city; and Wesley reads the falling on the face as being overwhelmed and, as it were, swallowed up.

The entry of the glory into the house is read by Gill as a taking of possession. The house has been described and measured, and now, being fitted and prepared, its builder and owner comes and takes up his residence in it, as Christ will do in his church, more visibly in the latter day. Wesley sets the return against the departure: the sins of Israel caused the glory of the Lord to go out of his house, and now the repentance of Israel is blest with the return of that glory.

Being lifted into the inner court draws out the widest difference of scale. Ellicott gives the plain reason: having seen the divine glory enter by the eastern gate, the prophet, himself a priest, is brought into the court of the priests, and there sees the glory fill the house as of old. Gill makes the same point about the priesthood, that none but priests went into the inner court, but frames the lifting as an act of grace, since the prophet lay on his face until a wind came, as the word signifies, or the Holy Spirit, which is compared to the wind for its invisible and irresistible power; humble souls are regarded by the Lord, who raises them up and brings them into nearer communion with himself and gives them clearer views of the glories of Christ. Clarke takes the same verb and runs it forward through the history of the church, asking how many men this heavenly Spirit has taken up, filled with his own influence and sent to every nation and tongue and people to testify the Gospel of the grace of God and to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and what spiritual temples have been raised and beautified and filled with the glory of God, a light shining more and more unto the perfect day when the whole earth shall be filled with that glory.

Who speaks and who stands are handled separately. Gill takes the speaker to be the Father, whose glory had entered the house, uttering his voice out of Zion, and adds that he speaks in his church by his word and the ministers of it, which is to be heard and regarded not as the word of man but as the word of God. Ellicott notes that although the pronoun is not expressed in the original there can be no question that God himself spoke directly to the prophet. On the man standing by, Wesley says flatly that it is Christ, standing to encourage and strengthen him. Ellicott is more cautious: the word is without the article in the Hebrew, which leaves it uncertain whether the same being is meant who had hitherto guided the prophet, though since measurements were afterwards made by that guide he was probably the same.
7:
Henry reads the speech from the house as a renewal of covenant, with the prophet negotiating the matter as Moses formerly; it would be of great use to the captives at their return for direction and encouragement, but looks further, to those blessed with the privileges of the gospel-temple. God begins by putting them in mind of their former provocations, a conviction spoken to make way for the comforts designed them, since though God forgives and upbraids not, it becomes us to upbraid ourselves. Gill leaves open whether the words are those of the man standing by, as the Arabic version has it, or of Jehovah speaking out of the house; Wesley says simply that it is the glorious God of Israel. On the throne and the soles of the feet Clarke distinguishes majesty from condescension in dwelling among men; Wesley takes the throne as the throne of grace and the feet as expressing his abode and rest in the temple as the type and in his church as the antitype.

The carcases of their kings are explained four ways. Clarke takes them literally: God was displeased at their bringing kings so near his temple, David having been buried in the city of David near to it, and almost all the kings of Judah likewise, whereas God requires the vicinity of his temple to be kept unpolluted. Wesley suggests instead that some kings were buried in the temples of their idols, near the idols they worshipped. Henry makes the carcases the images themselves, which they called their kings, for so Moloch signifies, or their lords, for so Baal signifies, but which were really lifeless and useless, loathsome and abominable as dead carcases. Ellicott reaches the same sense by argument, setting aside the literal reading since there is no historical proof that any king was buried in the Temple area, the gardens of the royal palace being too distant for the language used; the simplest explanation is that the language rests on an older statute and means idols, which Manasseh and others had introduced into the very courts.

The threshold set by God’s threshold is read on two levels. Clarke and Wesley keep it concrete: they had set up their idol altars beside those of Jehovah, so that their abominable idols were found in the very house of God, the kings of Judah and Israel having built temples for their idols in the courts or near them. Ellicott adds what the margin gives, that there was but a wall between God and them. Gill and Henry both take it of doctrine. Gill makes the threshold the way of entrance, so that whenever men open any other way into the house of God than he has directed they set their threshold by his: the way into the church is Christ himself and faith in him, and to make carnal descent or religious education or mere morality the way into church communion is opposite to God’s way. Henry says the same of the posts: it was adding their own inventions to God’s institutions and urging compliance with them as if they were of equal authority and efficacy, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.

Ellicott twice corrects the mood of the verbs: what the version renders as a command is in both places a simple future, in keeping with the ideal character of the vision, so that the house of Israel will put away their abominations and God will dwell in their midst for ever. That dwelling is for him the peculiar distinction of this temple, since the tabernacle and the temple of Solomon had each been accepted as the dwelling-place of God and each had passed away, as would the material temple of the restoration; only of this one is the promise for ever. Gill takes the whoredom to be put away as idolatry, superstition and will worship.
10:
What is shown, and to whom, divides the readers at once. Gill takes the house to be the one the prophet had seen measured, which he was bid at the outset to observe so that he might show it to others, and takes it to be no other than the Gospel church in its perfection and glory in the latter day. As for the hearers he offers two: the captives in Babylon among whom the prophet was, to comfort them with a view of what would be hereafter and at the same time humble them, or else the Jews in the first times of the Gospel, the prophet standing for the apostles. Ellicott keeps it inside the vision: the command is to make known to the people the new Temple and its appointments, that seeing God’s gracious purposes they may repent. Wesley narrows the audience to the rulers, prophets and priests especially, not excluding others, and reads the shame as what they shall feel when they blush to see what glory their iniquities had ruined.

Clarke draws the sharpest point from it. Let them be shown this holy house where the holy God dwells, that they may be ashamed; their name, profession, temple and religious services all bound them to a holy life, and all within and without them should have been holiness unto the Lord, yet they have been bound by no ties and have sinned against all their obligations. Nevertheless, he says, let them measure the pattern and measure themselves by that standard and walk accordingly. Ellicott reads the same clause as a charge to consider and follow out the provisions God had made for their worship, since exactness in observing all positive enactments is a necessary result of a desire to serve God.

On the condition attached to the fuller teaching the three agree in substance. Gill has the particulars shown only to those made sensible that what they had done was sinful, or at least not answerable to the pattern set before them, and who acknowledge it with shame; to penitent persons, he says, more grace and light and judgment in divine things are given. Clarke puts the same conditionally: if in a spirit of true repentance they acknowledge their past transgressions and purpose in God’s help never more to offend, then let them be taught everything that concerns his worship. Ellicott looks at the grammar and notices that what had been declared positively is now expressed contingently, which shows that the sanctification of the people and God’s dwelling among them were correlative facts, neither able to stand without the other; expressions of nearly the same meaning are heaped up later in the verse to press the significance of the new arrangements on the thought of the people.

The law of the house is read two ways. Gill calls it the general law that comprehends the rest, and Ellicott observes that the command to keep everything is closed, as often, by a summary statement of the reason: the whole surroundings of the dwelling-place of the Most High are holy. Clarke presses the summary to its limit: from the top of the mountain on which the house stands to the bottom, all round about, all shall be holy, with no buildings erected in any part and no place or spot appropriated to a common use, the whole being considered as most holy. Wesley keeps a degree of difference, granting that the whole circuit of the mountain shall be holy but making the top on which the temple stands most holy; and he reads the rule as saying that holiness becomes God’s house, this relative holiness pointing to personal and real holiness. Ellicott closes by noting that a new part of the vision begins with the following verse, describing the ordinances of the sanctuary, fitly opened with the altar, the central thing in the ancient worship.
13:
The measures open with the cubit, and the two who convert it do not agree. Clarke says it is the same cubit by which all the previous admeasurements were made, a handbreadth or four inches longer than the Babylonian cubit; Wesley calls it the sacred cubit, makes the excess three inches, and reckons the whole at twenty-one inches, broad enough for the priests to walk on. Ellicott sets the altar beside its rivals: its base was sixteen cubits square and its entire height either eleven or twelve, where the altar in Solomon’s Temple was of brass, twenty cubits square and ten high, and the one in the Temple of Herod, of hewn stone, thirty-two cubits square and ten high. The dimensions here seem to him chosen for symmetry, and in height this altar exceeded any of the others. Gill and Clarke both make it ten cubits high, Gill noting that some make it eleven.

Henry converts the whole into yards and finds a lesson in the arrangement. It was six yards square at the top and seven at the bottom and four yards and a half high, with a settle a yard from the ground on which some priests stood and another two yards above it on which others stood, each half a yard broad and railed with ledges that they might stand firmly. The sacrifices were killed at the table spoken of earlier; what was to be burnt was given to those on the lower bench and handed by them to those on the higher, who laid it on the altar. Thus in the service of God, Henry says, we must be assistant to one another. Gill reads the altar as a type of Christ with respect to his deity, which is greater than the sacrifice of his human nature and is the support of it, sanctifying it and rendering it acceptable; and he finds in the twelve cubits each way the doctrine of the twelve apostles.

Three of them handle the names given to the parts. All note that the altar proper is called Harel, the mountain of God; Gill says it was so called because for its size it looked like a mountain standing in the court, and adds that it was on a mountain that Christ was offered up. Clarke finds two words rather than one, the mount of God and, in the next clause, the lion of God, taking the first for the altar as elevated to the honour of God and the place where victims were offered, and the second for the hearth, so called because it devoured the burnt-offerings as a lion does his prey. Ellicott, who lays the parts out in order, corrects one rendering: where the version has higher place the word should be base, since it means primarily arched, then a back, then a support.

What the settle of the last verse is, and how the priests got up, are the two open questions. Gill reports that Kimchi confesses his ignorance here, follows Jarchi in taking it for the top of the altar with the horns and the priests’ standing-place, and holds him right against those who make it the lower settle: it is the hearth where the sacrifice was burnt, with a projection of a cubit on each side making the twelve cubits fourteen. Clarke takes it for the ledge on which the priests walked round the altar, and observes that by these ledges the altar was narrowed towards the top, the older altar of burnt-offering, he adds, was smaller because it had to be moved with the tabernacle, whereas this was designed for a permanent temple. On the going up the two part company: Wesley speaks of stairs or steps, each perhaps about a quarter of a cubit, to carry them up to the first and second settles, while Clarke says the ascent was an inclined plane.
18:
The statutes of the altar are introduced with a phrase Ellicott thinks worth pressing. The words about the day when they shall make it look to the future, implying that the whole structure of the Temple and its acceptance by the manifestation of the divine glory, though represented in the vision as already done, were still to come; the phrase is meant only to require that the altar be consecrated before it is used, and the time the consecration actually occupies is seven days, as under the older law. Gill notes only that this is the same voice continuing to speak to the prophet out of the house.

The priests who are to receive the altar are identified two ways. Clarke keeps to the history, that it was this Zadok who was put in the place of Abiathar by Solomon, and in whose family the priesthood had continued ever since. Gill gives the same fact and reads through it: the name signifies a righteous one, and he was a type of Jesus Christ the righteous, so that his seed signify the seed of Christ, those whom he makes priests unto the Lord; to these the prophet was to give this altar, for them to serve at and eat of.

Whether the prophet himself does any of this is raised by both Gill and Ellicott, and answered the same way. Ellicott says he is not actually to consecrate, as Moses did, but is told, as frequently in prophecy, to do that which he foretells is to be done. Gill reaches it from the history: the prophet was indeed a priest, but this must be understood in a visionary way, since, as Kimchi observes, he did not live to come up out of the captivity but died in the land of Babylon. Gill sets aside the same writer’s further suggestion that the passage is to be understood of the resurrection of the dead, with the prophet then serving as high priest, or as deputy to Aaron.

Ellicott notices twice what the passage leaves out. In the case of the altar of the Tabernacle the consecration began with anointing with oil, a prominent feature of that service, but here it is wholly omitted; and nothing is said of pouring the rest of the blood at the foot of the altar, as the law required, nor of burning the fat upon it. His explanation is that the prophet supposes the ritual of the sacrifices to be well known and mentions only a few particulars to indicate the whole, with a few others now introduced that are peculiar to the new ceremonial. What the service does begin with he thinks significant: a sin offering, which by the law was always offered first when several kinds of sacrifice fell together, since the first act of a man’s approach to God must consist of the confession of his sin.

Where the bullock is burnt is the one place the readers part. Wesley puts it in the court of the house and on the altar appointed, and marks it as the first day’s sacrifice, the priest being the one who burns it. Ellicott holds that it cannot be there. The flesh of ordinary sin offerings was to be eaten by the priests, but when the victim was a bullock, as for the high priest or the whole congregation, it was to be burned outside the camp; here it is to be burned in the appointed place of the house and yet without the sanctuary, that is, outside the Temple building, so that it must have been in the separate building described earlier. Gill says only that the prophet was to take the bullock out of the herd, separate it from the rest for this purpose, and deliver it into the hands of one of the priests.
22:
The ritual here is not that of the older law, and the fact is used two ways. Gill reports Jarchi observing that the goat of the second day was not in the tabernacle but is ordered for a future time, another ram having been appointed in its place by the law, and draws the inference that the ceremonial law is changeable and now abolished; the goat, he adds, was typical of Christ, without spot or blemish and yet figured by that animal as being made sin for his people. At the seven days he reports Kimchi owning the same difficulty, that this was not according to the order of Moses nor done by those who came up out of the captivity, so that a change in the order of sacrifices must be looked for. Clarke takes the opposite view of the same particulars. These are in general ordinances of the Law, he says, and the directions are given so that the people might follow them when put in possession of their own land; in several cases the prophet enters into particulars as if he had supposed that the book of the law had perished.

Ellicott lists the differences without drawing either inference. The animal of the second day is more exactly a buck of the goats, the sin offering prescribed for a ruler, and the phrase about doing as they did with the bullock implies that the ritual and the burning were the same; but at the consecration of the older altar a bullock was required on each of the seven days, and for the priests as well as the altar. So too the burnt offering, here a bullock and a ram where the older account has two rams; and with the salt, since the word rendered cast means throw or pour, indicating a more copious use than the seasoning the law ordains. Wesley finds in that salt an allusion to the perpetuity of the covenant made by sacrifice, and reads the command to offer as a direction to the priests rather than something the prophet does himself.

The order of the days is his other concern. Making an end of cleansing does not mean an end of the whole service of consecration but only of the sin offering for that day, since a later verse says distinctly that both a sin offering and a burnt offering fell on each of the seven. The burnt offering is not mentioned on the first day, he explains, because the sin offering changes on the second, so the prophet describes that for both days and then turns to the other, which remained the same throughout. Gill keeps the sequence more simply, the altar cleansed by the bullock and the kid on the first and second days and the rest following on the third.

The last clause turns on a reading of the text. Ellicott notes that the version follows the Masoretic emendation, whereas the literal translation of the text as it stands is that they shall fill its hand, the hand being the altar’s. To fill the hand is a synonym for consecration, commonly applied to the priests, who were consecrated by having the gifts they were to offer placed in their hands; Ellicott prefers to keep the unemended text, filling the hand of the altar being a strong figure for its being always supplied with sacrificial gifts. He observes that nothing is said in the passage of consecrating the priests, that family having been consecrated once for all by the older ceremonies. Gill takes the seven days of purging as denoting the perfect purity of the altar, and reads the offerings as made upon the altar of burnt offering that stood before the house where Jehovah dwelt. Wesley closes on the promise: those who give themselves to God shall be accepted, their persons first and then their performances, through the mediator.
